title: Hikers deploy bear spray in close encounters with bold grizzly in Banff National Park, Parks closes campgrounds
excerpt: “It has reportedly gained access to two backpacks, been involved in multiple close encounters where bear spray has been deployed, and recently, was reported to have damaged an unoccupied tent in the Hidden Lake campground."
content:
“It has reportedly gained access to two backpacks, been involved in multiple close encounters where bear spray has been deployed, and recently, was reported to have damaged an unoccupied tent in the Hidden Lake campground."

LAKE LOUISE – Parks Canada wildlife managers are keeping close tabs on a brazen young grizzly bear and hope it will den for the winter without any further close encounters.

The wildlife team has been monitoring the behaviour of this bold sub-adult grizzly bear in the remote Skoki region of Banff National Park since putting a bear warning in place on Sept. 2.

James Eastham, a spokesperson for Lake Louise, Yoho and Kootenay field unit, said campgrounds at Hidden Lake and Baker Lake are now also closed because the bear’s behaviour has been escalating over this time.

“It has reportedly gained access to two backpacks, been involved in multiple close encounters where bear spray has been deployed, and recently, was reported to have damaged an unoccupied tent in the Hidden Lake campground,” he said.

It is not known if the grizzly bear is male or female.

Eastham said Parks Canada must consider the full range of accepted wildlife management tools when managing wildlife.

He said the approach prioritizes prevention, early intervention, and adaptive management, supported by ongoing monitoring of wildlife populations and behaviour.

“At this point in the season, the weather is no longer suitable for trapping and collaring the animal,” he said.

“Parks Canada’s wildlife management staff will continue to monitor the bear’s behaviour until it has denned for the winter and will evaluate potential management options that could be used in spring 2027.”

Bears are active on the landscape throughout most of the year.

Parks Canada reminds people to follow safe practices when in the national park, including traveling in groups whenever possible, and making noise regularly by calling out rather than relying on bear bells.

Dogs must be kept on a leash at all times, or people can consider leaving them at home as an option, too. Carry bear spray, have it accessible and know how to use it.

Report wildlife sightings, and any signs of illegal camping activity or unattended food or garbage by immediately calling Banff National Park 24/7 Dispatch at 403-762-1470.
